lines: Morgan Kim
+1 (555) 010-8173 | morgan.kim@example.com | example.com/code/mkim
EDUCATION
Clearwater Institute of Technology | B.S. in Electrical Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2017 - May 2021
EXPERIENCE
Voltline Robotics | Embedded Software Engineer | Metro City, USA | Mar 2023 - Jun 2025
- Improved update speed by 60% by compressing firmware images and resuming interrupted downloads.
- Wrote a hardware-in-the-loop test rig that ran 400 motor-control tests on every firmware build.
- Added a crash logger that saved the last 2 seconds of sensor data to flash, which found the root cause of 5 field failures.
- Sampled the motor's 5 kHz vibration signal at 8 kHz so the fault detector could capture it without aliasing.
- Fixed a race condition on the counter shared by the interrupt handler and the main loop by declaring the counter volatile.
- Rewrote the motor-controller firmware for a warehouse robot fleet of 300 units, cutting control-loop jitter from 120 to 15 microseconds and field motor faults by 60%.
Clearwater Sensors | Hardware Test Engineer | Metro City, USA | Apr 2022 - Feb 2023
- Automated end-of-line tests for a humidity sensor, cutting test time per unit from 90 to 25 seconds across 20,000 units a month.
- Traced a batch of early field failures to a solder-paste change; the findings updated the reflow profile and cut returns from 2.1% to 0.4%.
- Wrote the calibration procedure for the sensor line, cutting calibration drift complaints from 15 to 2 a quarter.
- Designed a test fixture that checked 8 boards at once, raising station throughput from 40 to 150 boards an hour.
PROJECTS
Low-Power Weather Station | Independent Project | C, STM32 | Jan 2025 - Present
- Engineered a next-generation, innovation-driven IoT solution that redefines sustainable environmental sensing.
- Cut average current from 4.2 mA to 0.9 mA by sleeping between readings and batching radio transmissions.
- Published the schematics and firmware openly, and a local school built two stations from them.
Formula Student Electric Car | Electronics Lead, Team of 12 | C | Sep 2019 - May 2021
- Worked on firmware and testing for the robot fleet's motor controllers.
- The CAN-bus firmware for the dashboard was written and tested against the motor controller before each race.
- Rewrote motor-control firmware for a fleet of about 300 robots, cutting control-loop jitter eightfold and motor faults by more than half.
SKILLS
Tools: C, C++, STM32, oscilloscopes, FPGA
Methods: firmware, hardware-in-the-loop testing, CAN, low-power design

items.says: The code URL should lead directly to a polished profile or repository, not a generic landing page.
items.because: A direct link makes the work easier to assess.

items.says: Label the code-hosting platform if it is GitHub.
items.because: The label may improve scanability.

items.says: Prominently feature the weather-station project and other embedded work at the linked destination.
Use city and state rather than “Metro City, USA” for U.S. applications.
Confirm that the June 2025 end date is accurate and change it if the role is ongoing.
items.because: If the role ended, the period afterward may need explaining.

items.says: Define what “update speed” measures.
items.because: It could mean total time, transmission time, effective throughput, or something else.

items.says: Verify what caused the 60% improvement.
items.because: Resuming interrupted downloads improves recovery but does not necessarily speed up a normal update.

items.says: Separate compression and resume/recovery results if they have distinct metrics.
Add implementation context, such as the communication channel or device constraints, if space allows.
Clarify whether you built physical hardware, wrote test software, or did both.
items.because: “Test rig” can imply either.

items.says: Add a practical result of the testing, if available.
items.because: The number of tests alone does not show the effect on time, releases, defects, or coverage.

items.says: Clarify what the 400 tests count.
items.because: They could be test cases, parameterized executions, or hardware scenarios.

items.says: Change the wording that says the logger found root causes.
items.because: A logger records evidence; an engineering investigation identifies root causes.

items.says: Clarify whether the five field failures were incidents or distinct failure modes.
items.because: Distinct failure modes would be a stronger accomplishment.

items.says: Mention relevant flash, timing, or memory constraints if applicable.
Sampling a 5 kHz signal at 8 kHz cannot ordinarily capture it without aliasing.
items.because: 8 kHz is below the 10 kHz Nyquist rate.

items.says: State the actual sampling or signal-processing method if it was something other than ordinary sampling.
items.because: Deliberate undersampling, mixing, envelope detection, or a higher internal rate could change the explanation.

items.says: Clarify what “5 kHz” describes.
items.because: It could be a frequency, bandwidth, sensor output rate, or another quantity.

items.says: Declaring the counter `volatile` does not fix a race condition.
items.because: It does not provide atomicity, mutual exclusion, or ordering between the interrupt and main loop.

items.says: Describe the actual synchronization mechanism, if one was used.
items.because: An atomic operation, critical section, interrupt masking, or safe access pattern could address the issue.

items.says: Reassess the diagnosis if `volatile` was the only change.
items.because: The issue may have been a stale read or optimization issue rather than a race condition.

items.says: Move the fleet firmware result to or near the top of the Voltline bullets.
items.because: It combines scale, technical difficulty, and two strong outcomes.

items.says: Clarify what the 300 units represent.
items.because: They could be concurrently deployed units, the installed base, or cumulative production.

items.says: Specify how and over what period jitter and field faults were measured.
Verify that the fault reduction can reasonably be attributed to the firmware rewrite.
Make relevant manufacturing or sensor-technology context visible in the section, if applicable.
Clarify what the 20,000 units per month represent.
items.because: They could be total line volume or units processed by your automation.

items.says: Add the test platform or automation technology if relevant to target jobs.
Confirm that the shorter test time did not sacrifice coverage.
items.because: Interviewers may ask about that tradeoff.

items.says: Clarify the period and definition of the reported returns percentages.
items.because: They could refer to a return rate, failure rate, or specific defect category.

items.says: Be able to explain how the solder-paste change was isolated from other variables.
Identify your investigative contribution more precisely if you performed particular analyses or tests.
Clarify the measurement period and replace the informal “a quarter” with consistent rate terminology.
Substantiate the connection between the procedure and fewer complaints.
items.because: A written procedure alone may not explain the reduction without changes to equipment, sequence, limits, or training.

items.says: Define “calibration drift complaints.”
items.because: They could be customer complaints, internal quality events, or returned units.

items.says: Specify which parts of the fixture you designed.
items.because: It is unclear whether you designed its electrical, mechanical, electronic, or software components, or the complete system.

items.says: Add quality or reliability results if available.
items.because: Repeatability, false failures, or operator errors would provide further context.

items.says: Verify that the throughput comparison uses the same staffing and station assumptions.
Add other major relevant technologies actually used.
items.because: The radio protocol, PCB tool, sensor interface, or power-measurement method could add useful context.

items.says: Ensure the repository shows recent, meaningful activity while the project is marked “Present.”
Consider an end date if the project is functionally complete.
items.because: It may be more accurate than “Present.”

items.says: The buzzword-heavy bullet should be deleted.
items.because: Its promotional language provides no technical substance, evidence, ownership, or result and can reduce credibility.

items.says: Add the conditions under which average current was measured, if space allows.
items.because: Reading and transmission intervals, voltage, sleep duration, and equipment would clarify the metric.

items.says: Translate the current reduction into battery-life impact if defensible.
Identify the radio technology if it materially affected the optimization.
Confirm that 0.9 mA suits the application and that testing included all operating states.
Ensure the linked repository includes documentation and an appropriate license.
items.because: It should contain schematics, firmware, build instructions, and a bill of materials.

items.says: Clarify whether the school built the stations independently or with substantial hands-on help.
Mention active deployment if accurate and relevant.
Verify the “Electronics Lead” title and clarify the relationship to the 12-person team.
items.because: It is unclear whether you led all 12 members or worked within that team.

items.says: List other relevant technologies actually used, if applicable.
items.because: Listing only C may understate work with CAN hardware, PCB design, data acquisition, or microcontrollers.

items.says: The robot-fleet work does not fit the Formula Student electric-car project.
items.because: It appears copied from the Voltline role.

items.says: Replace the vague “worked on” wording with the actual car subsystem, your ownership, and the outcome.
items.because: The current wording obscures your responsibility and adds little value.

items.says: Use active voice and state what you personally designed, implemented, or validated.
items.because: The passive voice makes ownership unclear.

items.says: Explain what testing against the motor controller involved.
items.because: It could mean message compatibility, fault handling, timing, bus load, or hardware integration.

items.says: Replace “before each race” with a meaningful validation scope or result.
items.because: Frequency alone does not show effectiveness.

items.says: Add an outcome, if available.
items.because: Reliable operation, reduced integration time, or faults caught would show the work’s effect.

items.says: The 300-robot firmware result appears to duplicate the Voltline accomplishment.
items.because: The fleet size and outcomes are nearly identical, raising questions about copied metrics.

items.says: A 300-robot fleet is inconsistent with a Formula Student electric-car project.
items.because: The student work should describe its actual vehicle scope and project-specific results.

items.says: Resolve the inconsistent timeline created by the robot-fleet content under Formula Student.
items.because: That content appears to belong to the later Voltline role.

items.says: Reorganize the “Tools” line by type of skill.
items.because: It mixes languages, a microcontroller platform, test equipment, and hardware technology.

items.says: Specify FPGA languages and toolchains if you have real experience with them.
items.because: “FPGA” alone is too broad and may invite questions you cannot answer.

items.says: Add other meaningfully used tools and technologies where relevant.
items.because: Version control, debuggers, build systems, RTOS platforms, frameworks, scripting, PCB tools, or logic analyzers could be useful.

items.says: Order skills to match the target job rather than arbitrarily.
Reorganize the “Methods” line by type of capability.
items.because: It mixes a work product, a testing methodology, a protocol, and a design discipline.

items.says: Replace broad labels with more specific, defensible capabilities.
Avoid repeating concepts already evident in the experience section unless needed as ATS keywords.
Include other embedded capabilities only where supported by actual work.
items.because: Debugging, interrupt-driven and real-time systems, protocols, or automated testing could be relevant.

items.says: Use consistent date punctuation throughout the résumé.
items.because: Typographic dashes are preferable to hyphens.

items.says: Keep spacing, wrapping, and punctuation consistent, and avoid unnecessary bullet line breaks.
Use consistent unit formatting, including spaces between numbers and units.
